herbs.medicinalUses: Ginger preparations have been studied for nausea and vomiting in pregnancy. A small placebo-controlled trial reported symptom improvement over four days. This does not establish ordinary ginger tea as an equivalent treatment or support claims for every kind of nausea.
herbs.preparationMethod: The cited research used measured oral ginger preparations, not a standardized home tea recipe.
herbs.dosage: No home-treatment dose is provided. Discuss pregnancy-related nausea and any supplement with a qualified clinician.
herbs.warnings: Ginger can cause heartburn, abdominal discomfort, diarrhea, or mouth and throat irritation. Check for medicine interactions; breastfeeding safety information is limited.

evidenceReview.summary: 70 women randomized; oral ginger versus placebo for four days. Nausea and vomiting scores improved more with ginger.
evidenceReview.limitations: Small, short trial. The abstract cannot establish broad pregnancy safety, long-term outcomes, or tea equivalence.

reviewGaps: Full-text clinical appraisal and formulation verification

herbs.medicinalUses: A small trial of a turmeric extract reported reduced knee osteoarthritis pain over 12 weeks, but no improvement in the measured joint-fluid inflammation or cartilage composition. Results for a particular extract cannot be transferred directly to turmeric used in food.
herbs.preparationMethod: Research used a specific extract in capsules. Kitchen turmeric, isolated curcumin, and enhanced-absorption supplements are not interchangeable.
herbs.dosage: No home-treatment dose is provided; product composition and clinical suitability require professional review.
herbs.warnings: Turmeric supplements can cause digestive upset. Liver injury has been reported with some enhanced-absorption curcumin products. Stop use and seek care for jaundice or dark urine. Supplement use in pregnancy may be unsafe.

evidenceReview.summary: 70 adults randomized to extract or placebo for 12 weeks. Pain improved, but MRI effusion-synovitis and cartilage outcomes did not.
evidenceReview.limitations: Small single-center study, short follow-up and formulation-specific results; not proof of joint repair.

reviewGaps: Full-text clinical appraisal and formulation verification

herbs.medicinalUses: Malunggay leaves are used as food and studied for supporting milk production. Evidence summaries report possible benefit, but individual trials vary: an 88-participant trial did not find a statistically significant increase in milk volume on the third day after birth. Supplements do not replace breastfeeding assessment and support.
herbs.preparationMethod: The cited trial used leaf capsules. Cooked leaves and differently formulated supplements should not be treated as equivalent research preparations.
herbs.dosage: No general lactation dose is supplied. A health professional should assess feeding difficulties and the suitability of any supplement.
herbs.warnings: Long-term benefits and risks for breastfed infants remain insufficiently studied. Use caution with supplements if at risk of blood clots; discuss use with a clinician.
herbs.regionFound: Cultivated in Philippine backyards and farms.

evidenceReview.summary: 88 postpartum women randomized to leaf capsules or placebo. All completed the trial. Day-three milk volumes were not significantly different (p = 0.19). LactMed also discusses positive studies and meta-analyses.
evidenceReview.limitations: The single-center trial measured milk for one day, enrolled mostly cesarean-delivery patients, and excluded multiple higher-risk groups. One negative primary endpoint does not settle the entire evidence base. Formulations and populations differ; infant long-term outcomes remain uncertain.

reviewGaps: Qualified human content review of the full-text appraisal and comparative evidence

herbs.medicinalUses: Philippine traditional uses include leaf preparations for cough and digestive discomfort. These are records of use, not clinical proof of effectiveness. This plant is different from Mediterranean culinary oregano, Origanum vulgare.
herbs.preparationMethod: Traditional leaf preparations are documented, but this draft does not provide a clinically validated home recipe.
herbs.dosage: No verified human treatment dose is supplied in this batch.
herbs.warnings: Plant-specific safety, interactions, and use in children or pregnancy still require independent review. Do not use this draft as treatment guidance.

herbs.plantPart: Inner leaf gel; not latex or whole leaf
herbs.medicinalUses: A small acne trial found greater improvement with a prepared aloe gel plus tretinoin than tretinoin with its comparison gel. This supports further study of the combination, not a claim that raw aloe alone treats acne or all wounds.
herbs.preparationMethod: The study used a formulated topical gel alongside prescription treatment. Inner gel, yellow latex, and whole-leaf extracts have different safety profiles; no home extraction method is supplied.
herbs.dosage: No homemade or oral medicinal dose is supplied. Do not copy study formulations into a personal treatment plan.
herbs.warnings: Topical aloe can cause irritation or rash. Oral latex may cause cramps and diarrhea; oral leaf extracts have been linked to hepatitis. Oral use may be unsafe during pregnancy and breastfeeding. Do not infer oral safety from topical studies.
herbs.regionFound: Grown in Philippine pots and gardens.

evidenceReview.summary: 60 participants with mild-to-moderate acne in an eight-week randomized trial; formulated aloe gel plus tretinoin compared with tretinoin and vehicle.
evidenceReview.limitations: Small combination-treatment study; does not test aloe alone, raw leaves, or oral use.

reviewGaps: Full-text clinical appraisal and formulation verification

herbs.plantPart: Whole plant in Philippine documentation; extract in the cited trial
herbs.medicinalUses: A study in adults with diabetic wounds compared a standardized oral extract with placebo. Wound contraction favored the extract, while granulation-tissue formation favored placebo. The mixed outcomes do not justify treating diabetic wounds at home with this plant.
herbs.preparationMethod: Research used an extract capsule with measured asiaticoside content, not raw leaves or homemade tea.
herbs.dosage: No home-treatment dose is supplied. Diabetic wounds require professional assessment and care.
herbs.warnings: The selected trial excluded several higher-risk patient groups. Its short-term findings cannot establish safety for everyone. Independent safety and interaction review remains incomplete; do not use this draft to self-treat wounds.
herbs.regionFound: Occurs in the Philippines; documented in a North Cotabato plant study.

evidenceReview.summary: A randomized study enrolled 200 diabetic patients and examined wounds through day 21. Outcomes differed by wound measure. Philippine source uses the historical name Hydrocotyle asiatica.
evidenceReview.limitations: Only the clinical abstract was appraised. Safety cannot be inferred from brine-shrimp tests or the absence of serious events in a short trial.

reviewGaps: Independent safety review; EMA monograph discovered but download was rate-limited
